questions.q: Define half-life of a reaction. Write the mathematical expression for half-life of a first-order reaction in terms of its rate constant.
questions.a: Half-life (t₁/₂) is the time taken for the reactant concentration to fall to half its initial value. For a first-order reaction, t₁/₂ = 0.693/k (or ln2/k). A wrong answer (e.g., t₁/₂ = [R]₀/2k) reveals confusion with the zero-order formula, indicating the student memorized formulas without understanding their derivation from the integrated rate laws.

questions.q: Explain why the half-life of a first-order reaction is independent of initial concentration, whereas for a zero-order reaction it is directly proportional to initial concentration.
questions.a: For first order: ln([R]₀/[R]) = kt. At t₁/₂, [R] = [R]₀/2 → ln2 = kt₁/₂ → t₁/₂ = ln2/k (no [R]₀ term). For zero order: [R]₀ - [R] = kt. At t₁/₂, [R] = [R]₀/2 → [R]₀/2 = kt₁/₂ → t₁/₂ = [R]₀/(2k). A wrong answer reveals the student cannot derive half-life from integrated equations and relies on rote memorization.

questions.q: A first-order reaction has rate constant k = 2.5 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹. Calculate its half-life. If the initial concentration is 0.80 mol L⁻¹, what is the concentration after one half-life? After two half-lives?
questions.a: Step 1: t₁/₂ = 0.693/k = 0.693/(2.5×10⁻³) = 277.2 s. Step 2: After 1 half-life, [R] = 0.80/2 = 0.40 mol L⁻¹. Step 3: After 2 half-lives, [R] = 0.40/2 = 0.20 mol L⁻¹. A wrong answer (e.g., using zero-order formula or miscalculating 0.693/k) reveals confusion between order-specific formulas or arithmetic errors with scientific notation.

questions.q: For a zero-order reaction, half-life is 50 s when initial concentration is 0.20 M. If initial concentration is doubled to 0.40 M, what is the new half-life? Compare with a first-order reaction where half-life is 50 s at 0.20 M initial concentration.
questions.a: Zero order: t₁/₂ ∝ [R]₀, so new t₁/₂ = 100 s. First order: t₁/₂ independent of [R]₀, remains 50 s. A wrong answer (e.g., saying both remain 50 s or both double) reveals fundamental misunderstanding of the concentration dependence of half-life for different orders.

questions.q: A student claims: "For a first-order reaction, the time required for 75% completion is twice the half-life." Evaluate this statement with justification.
questions.a: The statement is correct. 75% completion means 25% reactant remains. After 1 half-life: 50% remains. After 2 half-lives: 25% remains. Thus time for 75% completion = 2 × t₁/₂. A wrong evaluation reveals confusion between "percentage completion" and "fraction remaining" — a common trap in competitive exams.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment using a colorimeter to determine the half-life of the iodide-catalyzed decomposition of hydrogen peroxide (first-order). Outline the procedure and how you would calculate half-life from the data.
questions.a: Procedure: Mix known concentrations of H₂O₂ and KI in a cuvette. Monitor absorbance at 230 nm (or use a suitable wavelength) vs time. Since absorbance ∝ [H₂O₂], plot ln(absorbance) vs time. Slope = -k. Calculate t₁/₂ = 0.693/k. Alternatively, directly note time when absorbance drops to half its initial value. A poor answer reveals inability to connect Beer-Lambert law (absorbance ∝ concentration) with integrated rate law.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Half-life of a ______ (t₁/₂) is the time required for the concentration of a reactant to decrease to exactly one-half of its initial concentration.
Fill in the blank: Imagine a doctor prescribing an antibiotic with a half-life of 6 hours — this ______ after 6 hours, half the drug is eliminated from your blood.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Student can derive half-life expressions for zero and first order reactions from their integrated rate laws, calculate half-life from given rate constant or concentration-time data, and explain why first-order half-life is concentration-independent while zero-order half-life varies linearly with initial concentration.
